claim: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are released by all cells into biofluids.
source: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are released by all cells into biofluids and hold great promise as reservoirs of disease biomarkers.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about EVs.

claim: EVs hold great promise as reservoirs of disease biomarkers.
source: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are released by all cells into biofluids and hold great promise as reservoirs of disease biomarkers.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential of EVs based on established scientific understanding.

claim: One of the main challenges in studying EVs is a lack of methods to quantify EVs that are sensitive enough and can differentiate EVs from similarly sized lipoproteins and protein aggregates.
source: One of the main challenges in studying EVs is a lack of methods to quantify EVs that are sensitive enough and can differentiate EVs from similarly sized lipoproteins and protein aggregates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations throughout the manuscript discussing limitations of existing methods.

claim: CD9, CD63, and CD81 are widely expressed transmembrane proteins.
source: Using Simoa to measure these three EV markers, as well as albumin to measure protein contamination, we were able to compare the relative efficiency and purity of several commonly used EV isolation methods in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): ultracentrifugation, precipitation, and size exclusion chromatography (SEC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tetraspanins that is also stated explicitly in the introduction.

claim: Simoa assays can measure CD9, CD63, and CD81 as EV markers.
source: Using Simoa to measure these three EV markers, as well as albumin to measure protein contamination, we were able to compare the relative efficiency and purity of several commonly used EV isolation methods in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): ultracentrifugation, precipitation, and size exclusion chromatography (SEC).
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and use of these assays throughout the study.

claim: Albumin can be measured to assess protein contamination in EV preparations.
source: Using Simoa to measure these three EV markers, as well as albumin to measure protein contamination, we were able to compare the relative efficiency and purity of several commonly used EV isolation methods in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): ultracentrifugation, precipitation, and size exclusion chromatography (SEC).
evidence: This is a methodological approach described and demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: EVs are released by all cell types.
source: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are released by all cell types and are found in biofluids such as plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about EVs.

claim: EVs are found in biofluids such as plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
source: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are released by all cell types and are found in biofluids such as plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge and is demonstrated by the experiments in the manuscript.

claim: EVs contain contents from their donor cells.
source: EVs contain contents from their donor cells, providing broad non-invasive access to molecular information about cell types in the human body that are otherwise inaccessible to biopsy (Hirshman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: EVs provide broad non-invasive access to molecular information about cell types in the human body that are otherwise inaccessible to biopsy.
source: EVs contain contents from their donor cells, providing broad non-invasive access to molecular information about cell types in the human body that are otherwise inaccessible to biopsy (Hirshman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: EVs are heterogeneous.
source: EVs are heterogeneous, present at low levels in clinically relevant samples, and difficult to quantify (Tkach et al., 2018; Hartjes et al., 2019; Shao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: EVs are present at low levels in clinically relevant samples.
source: EVs are heterogeneous, present at low levels in clinically relevant samples, and difficult to quantify (Tkach et al., 2018; Hartjes et al., 2019; Shao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: EVs are difficult to quantify.
source: EVs are heterogeneous, present at low levels in clinically relevant samples, and difficult to quantify (Tkach et al., 2018; Hartjes et al., 2019; Shao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is a lack of consensus about the best way to isolate EVs from biofluids.
source: Due to these challenges, there is a lack of consensus about the best way to isolate EVs from biofluids (Coumans et al., 2017a; Konoshenko et al., 2018; Théry et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), dynamic light scattering, and tunable resistive pulse sensing aim to measure both particle size and concentration.
source: These methods, such as nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), dynamic light scattering, and tunable resistive pulse sensing, aim to measure both particle size and concentration (Hartjes et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: NTA, dynamic light scattering, and tunable resistive pulse sensing cannot discriminate lipoproteins or particles of aggregated proteins from EVs.
source: A major limitation of these methods is that they cannot discriminate lipoproteins or particles of aggregated proteins from EVs (Coumans et al., 2017a; Sódar et al., 2016; Welton et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2019; Webber and Clayton, 2013; Johnsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Physical methods for measuring EVs provide no information about the biological nature of the particles being measured.
source: In addition, they are all physical methods that provide no information about the biological nature of the particles being measured.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of physical measurement methods.

claim: Biofluids, and plasma in particular, contain an abundance of lipoproteins and protein aggregates at levels higher than those of EVs.
source: Since biofluids, and plasma in particular, contain an abundance of lipoproteins and protein aggregates at levels higher than those of EVs (Sódar et al., 2016; Simonsen, 2017), these methods are ill-suited for quantifying EVs (Tkach et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Physical particle measurement methods are ill-suited for quantifying EVs.
source: Since biofluids, and plasma in particular, contain an abundance of lipoproteins and protein aggregates at levels higher than those of EVs (Sódar et al., 2016; Simonsen, 2017), these methods are ill-suited for quantifying EVs (Tkach et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and logical inference from the inability to discriminate EVs from contaminants.

claim: Lipid dyes bind to lipoproteins.
source: Lipid dyes have also been used to label and measure EVs (Osteikoetxea et al., 2015; Visnovitz et al., 2019), but these dyes also bind to lipoproteins and lack sensitivity (Tkach et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Lipid dyes lack sensitivity for EV measurement.
source: Lipid dyes have also been used to label and measure EVs (Osteikoetxea et al., 2015; Visnovitz et al., 2019), but these dyes also bind to lipoproteins and lack sensitivity (Tkach et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Obtaining quantitative measurements of EVs using flow cytometry remains challenging due to the small size of EVs.
source: There are also numerous efforts to apply flow cytometry to the analysis of EVs, but due to the small size of EVs, obtaining quantitative measurements using this approach remains challenging (Lucchetti et al., 2020; Kuiper et al., 2021; Welsh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Transmembrane proteins span the phospholipid bilayer of EVs.
source: A feature of EVs that distinguishes them from both lipoproteins and free protein aggregates is the presence of transmembrane proteins that span the phospholipid bilayer (Simonsen, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge about EV structure.

claim: The presence of transmembrane proteins distinguishes EVs from both lipoproteins and free protein aggregates.
source: A feature of EVs that distinguishes them from both lipoproteins and free protein aggregates is the presence of transmembrane proteins that span the phospholipid bilayer (Simonsen, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81 are transmembrane proteins that are widely expressed and readily found on EVs.
source: The tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81 are transmembrane proteins that are widely expressed and readily found on EVs, often referred to as 'EV markers' (Tkach et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: CD9, CD63, and CD81 are often referred to as 'EV markers'.
source: The tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81 are transmembrane proteins that are widely expressed and readily found on EVs, often referred to as 'EV markers' (Tkach et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: None of the tetraspanins CD9, CD63, or CD81 is present on every EV.
source: Although none of these proteins is present on every EV, measuring three tetraspanins should be a reliable proxy for EV abundance in many contexts.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about EV heterogeneity.

claim: Measuring three tetraspanins should be a reliable proxy for EV abundance in many contexts.
source: Although none of these proteins is present on every EV, measuring three tetraspanins should be a reliable proxy for EV abundance in many contexts.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim that is tested and supported by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ELISA lacks the sensitivity to detect low-abundance proteins.
source: The most commonly used method for measuring proteins in biofluids is enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), but this technique lacks the sensitivity to detect low-abundance proteins (Coumans et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Simoa technology converts ELISA into a digital readout.
source: Single-molecule array (Simoa) technology, previously developed in our lab but now commercially available, converts ELISA into a digital readout (Rissin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original Simoa publication.

claim: Simoa assays can be orders of magnitude more sensitive than traditional ELISAs.
source: Simoa assays can be orders of magnitude more sensitive than traditional ELISAs (Cohen and Walt, 2019), which is particularly useful for EV analysis as the levels of EV proteins are often low in clinical biofluid samples (Coumans et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The levels of EV proteins are often low in clinical biofluid samples.
source: Simoa assays can be orders of magnitude more sensitive than traditional ELISAs (Cohen and Walt, 2019), which is particularly useful for EV analysis as the levels of EV proteins are often low in clinical biofluid samples (Coumans et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: L1CAM is not associated with EVs in plasma and CSF.
source: We have previously applied Simoa to the investigation of L1CAM, a protein thought to be a marker of neuron-derived EV, showing it is not associated with EVs in plasma and CSF (Norman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: In Simoa, individual immuno-complexes are isolated into femtoliter wells that fit only one bead per well.
source: In Simoa, unlike in traditional ELISA, individual immuno-complexes are isolated into femtoliter wells that fit only one bead per well.
evidence: This describes the technical mechanism of Simoa technology.

claim: In Simoa, there are many more antibody-bound beads than target proteins in a given sample.
source: In a given sample, there are many more antibody-bound beads than target proteins, and therefore Poisson statistics dictate that only a single immuno-complex is present per well.
evidence: This describes the technical principle underlying Simoa.

claim: Poisson statistics dictate that only a single immuno-complex is present per well in Simoa.
source: In a given sample, there are many more antibody-bound beads than target proteins, and therefore Poisson statistics dictate that only a single immuno-complex is present per well.
evidence: This is based on statistical principles applied to the Simoa technology.

claim: Simoa allows counting 'on wells' as individual protein molecules.
source: This allows counting 'on wells' as individual protein molecules (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the principle of Simoa and is illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: The percentage of 'on wells' in Simoa can be converted to protein concentration by comparing to a calibration curve of recombinant protein standard.
source: The percentage of 'on wells' can then be converted to protein concentration by comparing to a calibration curve of recombinant protein standard.
evidence: This describes the quantification method used in Simoa.

claim: Simoa assays for CD9, CD63, and CD81 are 1–3 orders of magnitude more sensitive than the corresponding standard ELISA assays with the same pairs of antibodies.
source: We previously developed and validated Simoa assays for the proteins CD9, CD63, and CD81, showing that they are 1–3 orders of magnitude more sensitive than the corresponding standard ELISA assays with the same pairs of antibodies (Norman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: SEC separates EVs from free proteins based on size.
source: SEC separates EVs from free proteins based on size; proteins enter porous beads and elute from the column later than the EVs, which are much larger and less likely to enter the beads (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the principle of SEC and is illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: In SEC, proteins enter porous beads and elute from the column later than EVs.
source: SEC separates EVs from free proteins based on size; proteins enter porous beads and elute from the column later than the EVs, which are much larger and less likely to enter the beads (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of SEC separation.

claim: EVs are much larger than free proteins and less likely to enter SEC beads.
source: SEC separates EVs from free proteins based on size; proteins enter porous beads and elute from the column later than the EVs, which are much larger and less likely to enter the beads (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on the size difference between EVs and proteins.

claim: The Izon qEVoriginal 35 nm SEC column (collecting fractions 7–10) yielded both the highest recovery of EVs and the highest purity (ratio of EVs to albumin) of EVs in plasma.
source: In plasma, we found that the Izon qEVoriginal 35 nm SEC column (collecting fractions 7–10) yielded both the highest recovery of EVs and the highest purity (ratio of EVs to albumin) of EVs (Figure 2b–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2b-f.

claim: In CSF, ExoQuick yielded the highest recovery of EVs.
source: In contrast, in CSF, ExoQuick yielded the highest recovery of EVs while Izon qEVoriginal 70 nm yielded the highest purity (Figure 2g–k).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2g-k.

claim: In CSF, Izon qEVoriginal 70 nm yielded the highest purity.
source: In contrast, in CSF, ExoQuick yielded the highest recovery of EVs while Izon qEVoriginal 70 nm yielded the highest purity (Figure 2g–k).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2g-k.

claim: Resins with smaller pore sizes led to higher yields of EVs.
source: First, we found that resins with smaller pore sizes led to higher yields of EVs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data comparing different Sepharose resins.

claim: Sepharose CL-6B gave the highest yield of EVs among the tested resins.
source: Sepharose CL-6B, which has the smallest pore size, gave the highest yield, although it was accompanied by higher albumin contamination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Sepharose CL-6B was accompanied by higher albumin contamination.
source: Sepharose CL-6B, which has the smallest pore size, gave the highest yield, although it was accompanied by higher albumin contamination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Higher purity can be achieved by taking a smaller number of SEC fractions, albeit at the expense of lower EV yield.
source: For all SEC columns, higher purity could also be achieved by taking a smaller number of fractions (e.g., 7–9 instead of 7–10), albeit at the expense of lower EV yield.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing the distribution of EVs and albumin across fractions.

claim: Doubling the height of any given SEC column from 10 to 20 ml resulted in better separation between EVs and free proteins, leading to higher purity but lower EV recovery.
source: Additionally, we found that doubling the height of any given column from 10 to 20 ml resulted in better separation between EVs and free proteins, leading to higher purity but lower EV recovery (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Larger loading volumes led to lower purity in both plasma and CSF.
source: When we compared loading different sample volumes in a 10-ml Sepharose CL-6B column, we found that as expected, larger loading volumes led to lower purity in both plasma (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and CSF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: In plasma, the Sepharose CL-6B 10 ml column provided over twofold more EVs relative to the Sepharose CL-2B 10 ml column.
source: We found that, in plasma, the Sepharose CL-6B 10 ml column provided over twofold more EVs relative to the Sepharose CL-2B 10 ml column, but also sixfold more albumin.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In plasma, the Sepharose CL-6B 10 ml column had sixfold more albumin than the Sepharose CL-2B 10 ml column.
source: We found that, in plasma, the Sepharose CL-6B 10 ml column provided over twofold more EVs relative to the Sepharose CL-2B 10 ml column, but also sixfold more albumin.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In plasma, the Sepharose CL-4B 20 ml column had similar EV levels to that of Sepharose CL-2B 10 ml column but had sixfold less albumin.
source: The Sepharose CL-4B 20 ml column, on the other hand, had similar EV levels to that of Sepharose CL-2B 10 ml column in plasma but had sixfold less albumin (Figure 5a–e), demonstrating a large increase in relative purity (EV to albumin ratio) (Figure 5f).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In plasma, the Sepharose CL-4B 20 ml column demonstrated a large increase in relative purity (EV to albumin ratio).
source: The Sepharose CL-4B 20 ml column, on the other hand, had similar EV levels to that of Sepharose CL-2B 10 ml column in plasma but had sixfold less albumin (Figure 5a–e), demonstrating a large increase in relative purity (EV to albumin ratio) (Figure 5f).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In CSF, the Sepharose CL-6B 10 ml column led to a large increase in EV yield relative to the Sepharose CL-2B 10 ml column.
source: In CSF, the Sepharose CL-6B 10 ml column led to a large increase in EV yield relative to the Sepharose CL-2B 10 ml column (Figure 5g–k), but the Sepharose CL-4B 10 ml column did not lead to improved purity (Figure 5l).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In CSF, the Sepharose CL-4B 10 ml column did not lead to improved purity.
source: In CSF, the Sepharose CL-6B 10 ml column led to a large increase in EV yield relative to the Sepharose CL-2B 10 ml column (Figure 5g–k), but the Sepharose CL-4B 10 ml column did not lead to improved purity (Figure 5l).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: NTA and other methods developed for analysis of synthetic particles have been applied to EV detection.
source: Several techniques, such as NTA and other methods developed for analysis of synthetic particles, have been applied to EV detection (Hartjes et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The utility of NTA and similar techniques is hindered by an inability to differentiate heterogeneous EVs from other particles with overlapping size.
source: The utility of these techniques is hindered, however, by an inability to differentiate heterogeneous EVs from other particles with overlapping size, such as lipoproteins or aggregated protein particles.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim supported by the discussion of method limitations.

claim: The lack of reliable EV quantification has made previous studies comparing EV isolation methods difficult to interpret.
source: Thus, although previous reports comparing EV isolation methods Lobb et al., 2015; Helwa et al., 2017; Baranyai et al., 2015; Soares Martins et al., 2018; An et al., 2018; Stranska et al., 2018; Diaz et al., 2018; Kalra et al., 2013; Serrano-Pertierra et al., 2019; Gámez-Valero et al., 2016; Takov et al., 2019; Brennan et al., 2020 have yielded some useful insights, the lack of reliable EV quantification has made these studies difficult to interpret (Tkach et al., 2018; Coumans et al., 2017a; Ludwig et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The measurement of EV transmembrane proteins overcomes the limitations of EV quantification with particle detection methods.
source: The measurement of EV transmembrane proteins overcomes the limitations of EV quantification with particle detection methods.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim supported by the experimental approach and results.

claim: CD9, CD63, and CD81 are present on EVs but are not present in lipoproteins or free protein aggregates.
source: Since the transmembrane proteins CD9, CD63, and CD81 are present on EVs but are not present in lipoproteins or free protein aggregates, these tetraspanins can be used for relative quantification of EVs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the structure of EVs, lipoproteins, and protein aggregates.

claim: Tetraspanins can be used for relative quantification of EVs.
source: Since the transmembrane proteins CD9, CD63, and CD81 are present on EVs but are not present in lipoproteins or free protein aggregates, these tetraspanins can be used for relative quantification of EVs.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim that is demonstrated by the experimental approach.

claim: By detecting three different tetraspanins per sample with Simoa, the chance of measuring a rare subset of EVs is minimized.
source: Although not every EV necessarily contains a tetraspanin protein, by detecting three different tetraspanins per sample with Simoa, we minimize the chance that we are measuring a rare subset of EVs.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim about the experimental design.

claim: A strong correlation of the relative levels of the three tetraspanins in different SEC fractions was observed.
source: In the experiments reported here, we observed a strong correlation of the relative levels of the three tetraspanins in different SEC fractions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Simoa is particularly well suited for EV analysis due to the technology's high dynamic range, throughput, and sensitivity.
source: We used Simoa in this study, which is particularly well suited for EV analysis due to the technology's high dynamic range, throughput, and sensitivity.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim supported by the characteristics of Simoa technology.

claim: High sensitivity is often necessary for the low levels of EVs in human biofluids.
source: One could also follow a similar approach to the one we present here with traditional ELISA or other protein detection methods, but we find that high sensitivity is often necessary for the low levels of EVs in human biofluids.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experience and the data presented.

claim: Simoa can detect EV markers in cases where traditional ELISA cannot, such as SEC fractions of CSF.
source: We have previously shown in a direct comparison (using the same antibodies) that Simoa can detect EV markers in cases where traditional ELISA cannot, such as SEC fractions of CSF (Norman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: To obtain the purest EVs possible and separate EVs from lipoproteins, it is necessary to combine several techniques sequentially, such as density gradient centrifugation (DGC) and SEC.
source: To obtain the purest EVs possible (and separate EVs from lipoproteins), it has been demonstrated that it is necessary to combine several techniques sequentially, such as density gradient centrifugation (DGC) and SEC (Karimi et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Techniques such as DGC are not scalable to many samples and therefore not amenable to biomarker studies.
source: However, techniques such as DGC are not scalable to many samples and therefore not amenable to biomarker studies.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim about the practical limitations of DGC.

claim: SEC requires no instrumentation and allows one to run many columns in parallel.
source: SEC requires no instrumentation and allows one to run many columns in parallel.
evidence: This is based on the nature of SEC as a technique.

claim: Sepharose CL-6B is seldom used for EV isolation.
source: Our investigation of SEC parameters led us to improved methods for EV isolation; in particular, we found that Sepharose CL-6B, which is seldom used for EV isolation, yields considerably higher levels of EVs than either Sepharose CL-2B, the most commonly used resin (Monguió-Tortajada et al., 2019), or Sepharose CL-4B.
evidence: This is based on a review of the literature cited.

claim: Sepharose CL-6B yields considerably higher levels of EVs than either Sepharose CL-2B or Sepharose CL-4B.
source: Our investigation of SEC parameters led us to improved methods for EV isolation; in particular, we found that Sepharose CL-6B, which is seldom used for EV isolation, yields considerably higher levels of EVs than either Sepharose CL-2B, the most commonly used resin (Monguió-Tortajada et al., 2019), or Sepharose CL-4B.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data.

claim: Sepharose CL-2B is the most commonly used resin for EV isolation by SEC.
source: Our investigation of SEC parameters led us to improved methods for EV isolation; in particular, we found that Sepharose CL-6B, which is seldom used for EV isolation, yields considerably higher levels of EVs than either Sepharose CL-2B, the most commonly used resin (Monguió-Tortajada et al., 2019), or Sepharose CL-4B.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Sepharose CL-6B beads have a smaller average pore size (24 nm) compared to CL-4B (42 nm) and CL-2B (75 nm).
source: We attribute this result to Sepharose CL-6B beads having a smaller average pore size (reported [Hagel et al., 1996] to be 24 nm vs. 42 nm for CL-4B and 75 nm for CL-2B), leading to a lower probability that EVs will enter the beads.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The smaller pore size of Sepharose CL-6B leads to a lower probability that EVs will enter the beads.
source: We attribute this result to Sepharose CL-6B beads having a smaller average pore size (reported [Hagel et al., 1996] to be 24 nm vs. 42 nm for CL-4B and 75 nm for CL-2B), leading to a lower probability that EVs will enter the beads.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based explanation for the observed results.

claim: There is a tradeoff between EV yield and albumin contamination in SEC.
source: As there is a tradeoff between EV yield and albumin contamination, we envision different SEC columns will be suited for different applications.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing the relationship between yield and purity.

claim: A 10-ml Sepharose CL-6B column is the best choice for EV isolation from plasma or CSF when maximum EV yield is needed and some free protein contamination is not detrimental.
source: Using a 10-ml Sepharose CL-6B column for EV isolation from plasma or CSF is the best choice for downstream applications where maximum EV yield is needed and where some free protein contamination is not detrimental—for example, analyzing rare EV cargo or when further purification of EVs will be performed (such as immuno-isolation).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental results.

claim: A larger 20 ml column with Sepharose CL-4B would yield better results when isolating EVs from plasma where minimal free protein contamination is desired.
source: On the other hand, if isolating EVs from plasma where minimal free protein contamination is desired (e.g., in EV protein analysis by Western blot), a larger 20 ml column with Sepharose CL-4B would yield better results.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental results.

claim: For CSF, which has much less protein than plasma, 10 ml columns are preferable to 20 ml ones.
source: For CSF, which has much less protein than plasma, 10 ml columns are preferable to 20 ml ones.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental results comparing column sizes.

claim: Albumin is the most abundant protein in plasma.
source: By developing a Simoa assay to measure albumin (the most abundant protein in plasma and main contaminant when isolating EVs), we were able to assess the purity of EV preparations with respect to unwanted co-purification of free proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plasma composition.

claim: Albumin is the main contaminant when isolating EVs.
source: By developing a Simoa assay to measure albumin (the most abundant protein in plasma and main contaminant when isolating EVs), we were able to assess the purity of EV preparations with respect to unwanted co-purification of free proteins.
evidence: This is based on the abundance of albumin and the results of the experiments.

claim: Adding a Simoa assay for ApoB100 would allow for the assessment of both lipoprotein and free protein contamination in EV isolation methods.
source: Adding a Simoa assay for ApoB100 (or other protein components of lipoproteins) would allow for the assessment of both lipoprotein and free protein contamination in EV isolation methods.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future work.

claim: Lipoproteins are difficult to separate from EVs due to their overlapping size profile.
source: Although lipoproteins are difficult to separate from EVs due to their overlapping size profile (Simonsen, 2017), a recent study demonstrated that a chromatography column combining a cation-exchange resin layer with an SEC resin layer allows for efficient lipoprotein depletion using 'dual mode chromatography' (Van Deun et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: A chromatography column combining a cation-exchange resin layer with an SEC resin layer allows for efficient lipoprotein depletion using 'dual mode chromatography'.
source: Although lipoproteins are difficult to separate from EVs due to their overlapping size profile (Simonsen, 2017), a recent study demonstrated that a chromatography column combining a cation-exchange resin layer with an SEC resin layer allows for efficient lipoprotein depletion using 'dual mode chromatography' (Van Deun et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Simoa could be used to evaluate and help improve dual mode chromatography techniques in the future.
source: Simoa could be used to evaluate and help improve such techniques in the future.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future applications.

claim: The experimental framework presented could be easily applied to evaluate new EV isolation methods in plasma, CSF, or other biological fluids, such as urine or saliva.
source: The general experimental framework presented here could be easily applied to evaluate new EV isolation methods in plasma, CSF, or other biological fluids, such as urine or saliva.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future applications based on the demonstrated approach.

claim: Similar methods could be applied to compare EV isolation methods from cell culture media.
source: While we limited our study to human biofluids, similar methods could also be applied to compare EV isolation methods from cell culture media.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future applications.

claim: Sensitivity of EV detection and specificity in differentiating EVs from contaminants are obstacles in all EV studies.
source: As sensitivity of EV detection and specificity in differentiating EVs from contaminants are obstacles in all EV studies, we envision that ultrasensitive protein detection with Simoa will be broadly applicable to assessing EV isolation methods for both the study of EV biology and development of EV diagnostics.
evidence: This is based on the challenges discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ultrasensitive protein detection with Simoa will be broadly applicable to assessing EV isolation methods for both the study of EV biology and development of EV diagnostics.
source: As sensitivity of EV detection and specificity in differentiating EVs from contaminants are obstacles in all EV studies, we envision that ultrasensitive protein detection with Simoa will be broadly applicable to assessing EV isolation methods for both the study of EV biology and development of EV diagnostics.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on the demonstrated utility of the approach.

claim: All samples were centrifuged and filtered through a 0.45-μm filter to separate EVs from cells, cell debris, and large vesicles.
source: To separate EVs from cells, cell debris, and large vesicles, all samples were first centrifuged and then filtered through a 0.45-μm filter.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation method used in the experiments.

claim: Simoa has high reproducibility between technical replicates.
source: Since all Simoa measurements were performed with two technical replicates, we also confirmed that Simoa had high reproducibility between technical replicates (Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
